prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map depicts a room viewed from above where the camera wearer looks down at a carpeted floor with a black-and-white dog at the bottom center (about 1.0–1.5 m away), a plastic dog crate to the lower right (1.2–1.5 m away, within about 0.3 m of the dog), an armchair edge on the left (1.5–2.0 m), a flat-screen TV resting atop two wooden crates in the center (1.8–2.2 m away, partially occluding a bed 2.5–3.5 m behind it), and potted plants near a window on the right (2.0–2.8 m). In frame 1, the camera wearer's own left arm is extremely bright at the bottom-left edge within 0.3–0.5 m (well within arm's reach, while the dog and crate below require bending down to reach), and across frames 1 to 5 the camera wearer tilts, rotates counter-clockwise, and lowers toward the floor and the wooden crates under the TV, bringing the carpet and left crate within 0.5–1.0 m by frame 5 while the bed, armchair, and window exit the field of view. No other people are in the room, and the dog lies on the floor facing forward and slightly left away from the camera wearer, though it turns its head slightly left in frames 2–3 before being mostly cropped out at the bottom edge in frames 4–5. Compared to the RGB strip alone, the depth map clearly separates the foreground silhouette of the TV and its supporting crates from the similarly dark bed behind them and shows the continuous downward slope of the floor plane. However, the depth map becomes unreliable in frame 4 where the right side of the TV stand drops to pitch black (falsely indicating infinite distance) and in frame 5 where the angled carpet plane and wooden crate blur into an indistinct bright gradient.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates selected foreground and mid-ground objects against black across the room layout, detecting the camera wearer's left arm on the lower left in frame 1 (0.3–0.5 m away), the dog on the lower-center floor in frames 1–3 (1.0–1.5 m away, facing away from the camera wearer toward the TV), the back of the TV screen in the center of frames 1–2 (1.8–2.2 m away, above the floor crates), and two potted plants on the right (at 1.5 m on the dog crate and 2.5 m by the window, about 1.0 m apart). Only the camera wearer's own arm in frame 1 and the close carpet and crate in frame 5 are within immediate arm's reach (under 0.8 m), while the dog, armchair on the left, and TV stand sit 0.5–1.0 m apart from one another and are partially occluded or cropped at the frame borders as the camera pitches down and rotates clockwise relative to the floor across frames 3–5. While this map helps delineate the exact boundary of the dark dog against the dark crate opening in frames 1–3 and separates the upper plant foliage from its pot ('vase') against the overexposed window glare, it is highly unreliable in both class labels and spatial coverage. Specifically, it misclassifies the TV as a 'laptop' in frame 1 and 'suitcase' in frame 2, labels the dog as 'cat' (and splits it into two overlapping 'cat' masks in frame 3), hallucinates a 'banana' mask across the frame 2–3 boundary, and erroneously labels the entire ~0.5–1.5 m patch of grey carpet in frames 4–5 as a giant 'cat' with a tiny 'person' fragment at the bottom of frame 5 while completely missing the bed, wooden crates, armchair, and dog crate.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely blank across frames 1–3 and 5, containing only a single magenta hand skeleton in the upper-right quadrant of frame 4 where the back of the TV (about 1.2–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer) is located. Because the scene contains no people other than the camera wearer—whose left arm is briefly visible at 0.3–0.5 m on the bottom left of frame 1 and whose bare foot appears at the bottom-left edge of frame 4—there are no other human bodies facing or looking toward the camera wearer, and only the black-and-white dog lies 1.0–1.5 m away on the floor in front of the wooden crates. As the camera wearer bends down and tilts the camera toward the carpet and wooden crates from frame 1 to frame 5, bringing the floor and left crate within arm's reach (under 0.8 m) by frame 5, all human limbs remain either out of view behind the camera or cropped at the extreme lower-left border. The pose map offers no useful spatial information beyond what is visible in the RGB strip and is entirely unreliable here: it fails to detect the camera wearer's visible left forearm in frame 1 and foot in frame 4, and it hallucinates a compact right-hand skeleton on the plastic rear panel and mounting bracket of the tilted TV in frame 4.
